name: James the brother of the Lord
whenBasis: From Jesus' ministry to his stoning in AD 62, which Josephus dates to the interval between the governors Festus and Albinus.
summary: One of the brothers of Jesus, who did not believe in him during his ministry. The risen Jesus appeared to him. When Paul first went up to Jerusalem he saw James, the Lord's brother; Peter, freed from prison, sent word to James; at the council he gave the judgment that the Gentiles turning to God should not be troubled; and when Paul came to Jerusalem the last time, he went in to James and all the elders. Paul counts him one of the pillars. The letter of James opens in his name.
body: Jesus' family, including his brothers, once came to take custody of him, saying he was out of his mind. After the ascension his brothers are in prayer with the disciples. Paul says that men came from James to Antioch, and Peter drew back from eating with Gentiles.

later.text: Josephus says the high priest Ananus had “the brother of Jesus who was called Christ, whose name was James” stoned in AD 62. Hegesippus, as quoted by Eusebius, calls him James the Just and says his knees were hard as a camel's from praying in the temple.

Whether the brother of the Lord wrote the letter of James is debated. Joseph B. Mayor finds it in character with all Acts and Paul tell of James and in style with his speech and letter in Acts 15, and dates it before Paul's letters, which he takes to quote it. James Moffatt finds it hardly conceivable that James had the letter's Greek style and culture, notes that it never alludes to the resurrection or the messianic claims of Jesus, and dates it early in the second century.

sources.title: The Epistle of St. James: The Greek Text with Introduction, Notes and Comments
sources.author: Joseph B. Mayor
sources.note: ch. 7: 'the contents of the Epistle are entirely in harmony with the supposition that it was written by James the brother of the Lord … it agrees in style and diction with the speeches and letter of James literally recorded in the latter book'

sources.title: An Introduction to the Literature of the New Testament
sources.author: James Moffatt
sources.note: pp. 469–472: 'it is hardly conceivable that a man like James should possess the wide culture … and the power of literary expression and allusion which characterise this writing'; 'there is perhaps less violence done to the probabilities of the evidence, internal and external, upon the later hypothesis than upon any other'

traditions: by James: Joseph B. Mayor; Luke Timothy Johnson
by a later writer: James Moffatt

later.text: Jerome identified him with the apostle James son of Alphaeus, and his mother with the Mary who stood at the cross, the wife of Alphaeus and sister of Jesus' mother, and so held the Lord's brothers to be his cousins.

sources.title: Jerome, The Perpetual Virginity of Blessed Mary (Against Helvidius) 13–16

traditions: kept apart: Helvidius, whom Jerome answered
